Thank you, Madam Co-Chair, distinguished delegates, dear colleagues. Thank you for the opportunity to address the first meeting of this new subsidiary body. It's a true honor for the JEF Secretariat. The JEF has long recognized that indigenous peoples and local communities play a key role in addressing the world's environmental and developmental challenges. Today, I will discuss and focus on three key points that illustrate the lessons learned and the evolution of the GEF support to indigenous peoples and local communities, IPLCs. First point, support for IPLCs is not a safeguards issue. Obviously, the GEF has strong environmental and social safeguards standards, which all GEF projects must adhere to. This includes upholding the right to free, prior and informed consent. an obvious baseline requirement. But what we're discussing today is not how to avoid doing harm, it's how to support IPLCs to empower them to play their full role in the implementation of the coming Montreal global biodiversity framework. Second point is that supporting IPLCs effectively requires a range of complementary modalities. Over the past three decades, The GEF has provided financial support to IPLCs through the small grants programs, which will be presented by our colleague from UNDP, my neighbor here, in a minute. The GEF has also funded numerous country-driven projects where governments have decided to support IPLCs with their GEF allocation. These projects have led to policy and legal changes that no other funding modality would have enabled. These include Brazil's Indigenous Peoples Policy or the legal recognition of Indigenous Peoples and local communities conserved areas as part of the national protected area system in the Philippines. We are working to mainstream support to IPLCs in this larger portfolio of country-driven projects. The Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, the new fund we established to respond to the request of COP15, which we call the GBFF, includes engagement with and support to IPLCs as one of its seven project selection criteria. The GBFF Council has also decided to set a target that 20% of the entire GBFF funding should go to actions to support actions by IPLCs for biodiversity. We are proud today to share that countries and implementing agencies have responded to this call. Out of the more than 200 million US dollars already programmed under the GBFF, 32% is to support actions by IPLCs, which is far exceeding the target that was set. But the GEF recognizes at the same time the systemic barriers that limit access for IPLCs in purely country-driven projects. The GEF has thus decided in 2018 to create a dedicated budget line and mechanism for support to IPLCs. This led to the launch in 2022 of the US$25 million Inclusive Conservation Initiative, which is managed by IUCN and Conservation International. The Heart of Conservation Initiative led by WWF will provide an additional tranche of US$20 million of funding dedicated to IPLCs. It will be presented in a side event taking place at lunch break today in this very plenary hall. And finally, my third and last point, it is not just about the volume of financing, modality matters, including directness of access and self-determination of priorities. The GEF strives for a partnership approach that fully recognizes IPLCs as agents of change. That is why IPLCs have gained an enhanced role in the governance of the GEF itself. This includes the GBFF Council, which has two formal observer seats for IPLCs. It also includes the GEF Indigenous Peoples Advisory Group, which provides advice to the GEF Council and to the replenishment process. At the program level, the governance of both the Inclusive Conservation Initiative and the Art of Conservation Initiative is composed primarily of indigenous leaders. Together with the small grants program, these initiatives are meant to simplify access, reduce intermediaries, and support projects that are conceived, led, and managed by indigenous peoples and local communities themselves, including women and youth. The GBFF also emphasizes IPLC-led stewardship and governance of lands, territories, and waters. It is the first multilateral fund to track financial flows that supports actions by IPLCs. This is very different from assessing support where IPLCs are mere beneficiaries, and this is not easy to do consistently across countries and partners. That is why we're currently holding open discussions for guidelines on how to do this in practice. We will greatly welcome open discussion and input from participants here at this meeting, including by joining us for our side event or session on this matter on Wednesday at lunch break in the Africa room. In closing, Much remains to be done to improve the scale, accessibility and directness of funding for indigenous peoples and local communities. The GEF is committed to progress guided by and in partnership with indigenous peoples and local communities. Thank you, Madam Co-Chair.

Esteemed co-chairs, distinguished delegates, UNDP welcomes the opportunity to address the first session of the subsidiary body on Article 8j on the subject of indigenous peoples and local communities access to finance. UNDP implements a wide range of programs pertaining to planetary health, climate change, nature and indigenous peoples rights. These range from the UNDP Climate Promise, which supports states to increase the ambition of their nationally determined contributions in over 120 countries, support to the update of NBSAPs, assessment and implementation of national biodiversity finance plans, access to finance by indigenous peoples as part of the Jeff Small Grants Programme, the UN-REDD Programme, the UNDP Equator Initiative and related local action partnerships. UNDP recognizes that the global architecture for nature finance is complex, changeable and uneven. Nature and climate finance comprise a wide range of financial flows, investments and incentives to address the causes and effects of planetary health, conservation of forests, mangroves, peatlands, grasslands and oceans. The need for a fair and just energy transition, mechanisms to implement loss and damage, as well as locally led adaptation. The sources of nature and climate finance are both public and private and can be channeled through a wide variety of national, bilateral, multilateral and other funding arrangements, and increasingly through indigenous led funds. At the UN Permanent Forum in 2024, UNDP welcomed the report prepared by the former Permanent Forum Chair, Ms. Hindu Umaru Ibrahim, on the nexus between indigenous peoples and finance. UNDP further recognizes the work conducted by Charapa Consult on developing a set of common reporting parameters for direct access to finance by indigenous peoples. currently being beta tested by various philanthropic foundations, as well as engagement with the OECD DAC, which is mentioned in the background paper on a proposed set of policy markers, as well as the efforts by the former permanent forum chair, Dario Mejia, who is also on the panel, with whom we co-organized a session at the high level finance summit convened by President Macron in 2023. In this context, in 2018, the GEF Independent Evaluation Office prepared an analysis of the GEF's provision of finance to indigenous peoples, noting the primary importance of the SGP. The following year, in 2019, lessons learned from SGP partnerships with indigenous peoples, including a detailed analysis of direct access to grants, were prepared at the request of the former UN Special Rapporteur, Ms. Vicky Tauli-Corpuz. Building on the SUP modality, UNDP has mobilized additional bilateral agreements to channel finance to indigenous peoples and local communities, including the global support initiative to territories and areas conserved by indigenous peoples and local communities, now active in 55 countries for a total of $55 million financed by the government of Germany, which is in alignment with the Kunming-Montreal GBF targets 2021, 2022 and 2023. In conjunction with other international organizations and networks, UNDP is active in the Path to Scale Affinity Group convened after the COP26 to track the financial pledge of 1.7 billion in finance to indigenous peoples and local communities, which is expected to be renewed next month in Bellem with an increased commitment on direct access to climate finance, as well as a pledge on land tenure security. We need operational models that ensure indigenous self-determination, equitable access to research funding, and inclusion in decision-making are ensured. This leadership approach rejects deficit-based narrative and instead affirms indigenous strength, responsibility, and authority in shaping biodiversity solutions. Second, elevating indigenous knowledge systems. Our project creates ethical spaces where indigenous knowledge and science meet as equals, each guided by its own laws, languages, and world views. This approach enables new transdisciplinary innovations, bridging spirituality, ecology, health, and law to inform conservation policies that truly reflect Indigenous realities. Third, equitable access to research funding. Indigenous peoples have long been excluded from research systems that control knowledge and resources, and so the policy. Through the funding that we got from the new Research Frontier Fund, which is a Canadian national funding, we established a mechanism that directs research funds to indigenous governments, organizations and communities, ensuring they are not merely participants in research, but its rights leaders.
